title: Northeast coast · Ten states
intro: First, Clear removes the names from our western lesson. Today we follow ten Atlantic states, from Maine down to Virginia.
We'll start in New England, then move down the coast. I'll zoom in for the small states; their facts stay beside the map.

states.name: Maine
states.transition: Let's bring New England closer. Watch the northeastern corner move into view, with Maine reaching up toward Canada.
lines: Maine is our first stop: the big northeastern state, beside Canada. New Hampshire is its only neighbouring U.S. state.
The card offers two possible origins for Maine's name. One points to the French province; another to sailors referring to the mainland.
Its forest fact is memorable: close to nine-tenths of Maine's land is forested. Picture a wooded coast at the top of our route.

states.name: New Hampshire
lines: Follow Maine's southwestern edge into New Hampshire. Notice the small stretch that reaches the Atlantic; most of the state extends inland.
Its name comes from Hampshire in England. Another card fact recalls the Old Man of the Mountain, a rock profile that collapsed in 2003.
Keep the neighbours straight: Maine to the east, Vermont to the west, Massachusetts below. Vermont is inland, so we'll study it in another episode.

states.name: Massachusetts
states.transition: Let's zoom closer to southern New England. Massachusetts and the small states below it now have more room on the map.
lines: Now Massachusetts, directly south of New Hampshire. Follow its eastern coast around Boston and out toward the hook of Cape Cod.
The name comes from the Massachusett people. The card also mentions Harvard, founded in 1636: the oldest institution of higher education in the United States.
Use Massachusetts as our horizontal anchor. The two small states immediately below it are Rhode Island and Connecticut.

states.name: Rhode Island
lines: Here's Rhode Island, the tiny state below Massachusetts and just east of Connecticut. The whole state is more than the islands in its bay.
It's the smallest U.S. state by area. The card recalls its longer official name, which included Providence Plantations until voters shortened it in 2020.
For the map, remember the tiny coastal slot: Massachusetts above, Connecticut to the left. Small state, but worth a careful look.

states.name: Connecticut
lines: Slide west into Connecticut. It sits below Massachusetts, beside Rhode Island, with Long Island Sound along its southern edge.
Its name is linked to an Indigenous expression for the long tidal river. That gives us a landscape clue as well as a name to remember.
Our five coastal New England states are Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut. Next, we turn toward New York.

states.name: New York
states.transition: Let's move southwest, keeping a close view. New York is much larger than its famous city, and New Jersey and Delaware need room below it.
lines: This broad state is New York. Most of it extends inland, while Long Island projects into the Atlantic beside Connecticut.
The card takes us to the Erie Canal, opened in 1825. It connected the Hudson River with the Great Lakes, making an inland route to the coast.
Think of New York as the bridge between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic. New Jersey lies just below its southeastern corner.

states.name: New Jersey
states.transition: We'll move closer again for New Jersey and Delaware. The coast and the two bays are easier to distinguish at this scale.
lines: New Jersey is the narrow coastal state south of New York. Pennsylvania is inland to its west, across the Delaware River.
Its name comes from Jersey in the Channel Islands. Another fact brings us to Edison's Menlo Park laboratory, where his phonograph was invented in 1877.
Follow New Jersey's coastline south. Delaware Bay opens below it, pointing us toward the next small state.

states.name: Delaware
lines: Delaware is this small strip below Pennsylvania, across Delaware Bay from New Jersey. Maryland wraps around its western and southern sides.
Its First State nickname comes from ratification: Delaware was the first state to ratify the United States Constitution, on December 7th, 1787.
Keep Delaware Bay and Chesapeake Bay separate. Delaware lies east of the Chesapeake, on the peninsula it shares with Maryland and Virginia.

states.name: Maryland
states.transition: Now we'll widen the view toward Maryland, so its long western reach and the Chesapeake Bay are both visible.
lines: Maryland is the irregular state around the upper Chesapeake Bay. Notice its narrow western reach and its land on both sides of the bay.
Its name honours Queen Henrietta Maria. The card also recalls Fort McHenry: the flag seen there in 1814 inspired the words of The Star-Spangled Banner.
Use the Chesapeake as your landmark for Maryland. Virginia lies farther south, and we will move the map to see it properly.

states.name: Virginia
states.transition: One more move south brings Virginia fully into the study area. Watch its long western taper and the Atlantic coast on the right.
lines: Virginia is our tenth state, south of Maryland and north of North Carolina. West Virginia is a separate state on its inland side.
The name honours Elizabeth the First. Its other card fact explains a nickname: eight U.S. presidents were born in Virginia, more than in any other state.
We've reached the southern end of today's route. Keep Virginia below Maryland, with North Carolina waiting for a later lesson.

recap: Let's pull back and retrace the coast. New England first: Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut.
Then New York, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland and Virginia. Pause here and follow those ten states from north to south.
That's ten new states, bringing our lessons to eighteen states covered. The list is saved, so the next episode can continue without losing track.
